Thought: I need to determine how finely divided carbide materials react with air. Let me think about the chemistry of carbides.

Carbides are compounds of carbon with elements that are less electronegative than carbon. Common examples include calcium carbide (CaC₂), silicon carbide (SiC), and tungsten carbide (WC).

When materials are finely divided, they have a much larger surface area exposed to air, which can dramatically change their reactivity. For many reactive materials, being finely divided can make them pyrophoric - meaning they can spontaneously ignite in air at room temperature without an external ignition source.

Many metal carbides, particularly those of transition metals and alkali/alkaline earth metals, can be pyrophoric when finely divided. For example, calcium carbide reacts vigorously with moisture in air, and uranium carbide can be pyrophoric when finely divided.

The answer is C. Pyrophoric - finely divided carbides can spontaneously ignite in air due to their high surface area and reactivity.
